newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Loyal understudy Chernomyrdin gets crack at power.
newsitem.headline: Loyal understudy Chernomyrdin gets crack at power.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who was handed temporary control of Russia by Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday, is a loyal understudy who has been waiting in the president's shadow.
Chernomyrdin, 58, assumed Yeltsin's full powers, including control of Russia's nuclear arsenal, under a decree which the president signed shortly before his heart bypass operation.

If all goes according to plan, Yeltsin will annul the decree when he comes round and power will be Chernomyrdin's for only a few hours. If anything goes wrong, he could stand in for Yeltsin for three months until a new election is held.

Chernomyrdin has steered Russia through almost four years of tough economic reforms since Yeltsin appointed him in December 1992. Western leaders view him and Yeltsin as the guarantors of stability in the world's biggest country.

Chernomyrdin has been at pains not to create the impression that he is hungry for power, especially in the four months since Yeltsin was taken ill, and he has stood by the president through one crisis after another.
"Chernomyrdin showed himself to be just as I expected -- solid and reliable. He did not let me down in a single critical or tough situation," Yeltsin wrote in his 1994 autobiography.

The stout, balding Chernomyrdin had won a reputation as an efficient manager as the head of the state-owned natural gas monopoly Gazprom from 1989 until 1992. But he is viewed as a grey bureaucrat and is blamed by many for the hardships they have endured under reforms.
He allowed television cameras a glimpse of his softer side last month, when he was filmed playing billiards, dangling his grandson on his knee and tinkering with his private car at a state dacha.
Chernomyrdin's influence, along with that of Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, grew as Yeltsin prepared for surgery.

Standing in for the president, he chaired meetings of the influential Security Council and the advisory Defence Council. He took control of a commission trying to crack down on tax debtors and took on a bigger profile in the Chechnya crisis.
Chernomyrdin's task had been to balance liberal requests for fast reforms against conservative demands for slower changes.
A former Communist Party member, he surprised critics with his grim determination to press on with reforms after his promotion to prime minister.
He also proved a survivor, holding on to his job despite a series of crises, including a brief but dramatic crash in the rouble's value in October, 1994, which forced out several cabinet colleagues.

His government's tough monetary course has pushed down inflation but driven many companies close to bankruptcy. Taxes and wages go unpaid and millions of people struggle to survive on incomes well below the poverty line.
Chernomyrdin took a low profile in the early stages of Russia's military campaign in Chechnya, but became more closely involved as Moscow started to seek peace.

He personally intervened to help end a hostage crisis in the southern Russian town of Budennovsk and said last month he would go to Chechnya soon -- his first visit since the fighting started in December 1994. No date has been set for the trip.

Chernomyrdin sailed through a confidence vote in the State Duma lower house of parliament soon after the Budennovsk raid and he hung on to power after the Communist Party made large gains in a parliamentary election last December.
His centrist bloc, Our Home is Russia, won only just over 10 percent of the votes in the poll and is the second-largest party in the lower house after the communists.
Parliament reconfirmed him as prime minister last August.
Viktor Stepanovich Chernomyrdin, born on April 9, 1938, joined the Communist Party in 1961 and worked his way up to join the Central Committee's industry department. He left the party in 1991.
He worked in Russia's main oil-producing region, Tyumen, in western Siberia, from 1983 to 1985 and became gas industry minister in 1985 under Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.
He is married with two grown-up daughters and a son.
